items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
items.title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
items.title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

items.summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

items.summary: Low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs) are emerging as a key infrastructure for heterogeneous unmanned aerial systems that support concurrent services within a shared three-dimensional airspace. Their coexistence creates strong coupling among mobility, connectivity, and shared network resources, while heterogeneous services impose distinct and time-varying requirements. These interactions naturally form a dynamic non-cooperative game in which both operating conditions and coordination objectives evolve over time. Conventional optimization and learning-based controllers typically rely on predefined objectives, limiting their ability to adapt autonomously to changing service requirements and resource priorities. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical hybrid large language model (LLM)- multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture organized as a dual-loop structure. Specifically, an outer adaptation loop employs LLM-assisted game orchestration to interpret service requirements and operator intent, and reconfigure objectives and resource priorities, while an inner loop executes decentralized, parameter-conditioned MARL policies under the configured game. A logistics-monitoring case study illustrates how the proposed framework facilitates coordinated coexistence among heterogeneous services, adapting to evolving operating conditions without retraining the underlying MARL policies. Finally, we discuss key challenges and research directions toward scalable, trustworthy, and adaptive agentic LAWNs.
items.title: Agentic AI Networking for Heterogeneous Unmanned Aerial Systems in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA
items.title: ENZTRA demonstration dataset: reference-guided phytase redesign and kinetic-structural triage

items.summary: Benchmark package accompanying the manuscript “Failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems: residual-error decoupling, an attainable-accuracy bound and an identifiability benchmark”. The package contains: the exact solution of the beam–two-mass moving-load benchmark and the modal and RK4 reference baselines on the same grid; the training campaign with random seeds, network configurations, collocation densities, training budgets, measured wall-clock times, residuals and relative-L2 errors for every run; the inverse-problem (speed and load-amplitude) campaign with its identifiability verdict; the weights of the reference physics-informed network; and the scripts that regenerate every figure, table and number of the paper. It supports two results of the paper: the residual–error decoupling for moving singular sources, and the attainable-accuracy bound obtained by fitting the same architecture to the exact solution. All runs are seeded, so the accuracy–cost comparison reported in the paper can be re-derived without retraining.
items.title: Benchmark package — failure boundary of physics-informed neural networks for moving singular-source problems (v1.0)

items.summary: Measurement data and reproduction scripts for the parallel performance of peclet.flow 1.1.0 solving creeping flow through a periodic random sphere packing with the cut-cell immersed boundary method. One physical problem is measured on four ladders: weak scaling on 1–32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs at 384 3 cells per GPU, strong scaling of one fixed problem on 24–1536 AMD Genoa cores and on 1–32 H100 GPUs, and a geometry-free Taylor–Green control on the same grids. The weak ladder tiles one unit cell, so every rung is an exact periodic replication of the same problem and the physical observable is a single number that every rung must reproduce — not a scatter across independently packed beds. The record contains the driver, the geometry artifact and the script that generated it, the cluster provisioning and job scripts, the raw per-run JSON and logs, the analysis that produces the tables and figures, and a build census (toolchain, MPI, driver, wheel checksums) for every machine. The solver runs at its shipped 1.1.0 defaults, with one stated exception documented in the report, and each run records the momentum solver the solver itself selected. Scope. This record measures one implementation. It reports peclet.flow 1.1.0 and contains no data from any earlier version: it is a statement of what this release does, not a comparison against its predecessors. Runs were performed on the Dutch national supercomputer Snellius (SURF).
items.title: Parallel performance of peclet.flow 1.1.0: strong and weak scaling of a cut-cell immersed-boundary incompressible flow solver on Snellius (Genoa CPU, H100 GPU)

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.
tags: Cyber Threat Intelligence, Multi-Agent Systems, Large Language Models, Space Systems Security, MITRE ATLAS, AI Governance, Indirect Prompt Injection, ICD 203
items.title: Governing the Intelligence Loop: Architectural Mitigations for Epistemic Fragility in Autonomous Space-Cyber Threat Analysis

items.summary: This deposit contains the analysis code, fitted parameters, output files, audit records, supplements, and citation list supporting the working paper "Power-Law Claims in Production and Supply Networks: What Survives a Uniform Certification Audit" (version 16, September 2026, posted on SSRN) by Bruce Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0000-8324-4331) and Melissa Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0001-4919-0728). Melissa Rishel contributed the independent validation of the statistical analysis and the mathematical derivations. The audit applies the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman 2009 maximum-likelihood estimation protocol with semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing and likelihood-ratio tests against alternative distributions, together with the Broido-Clauset 2019 five-category corpus classification, to a verified population of 20 published power-law claims in the supply chain operational literature. Three widely cited datasets are re-analyzed. The manuscript reports four distributions: Acemoglu et al. 2012's sectoral input-output out-degree (BEA 1997 Use Table), Liu, Shen, Tan 2021's international trade product networks in both the out-degree and in-degree directions (BACI HS92 Y2024 current release, 1,217 networks), and Axtell 2001's US firm-size distribution (SUSB 2017, n = 5,996,900 firms via the Virkar-Clauset 2014 binned-data MLE). The Acemoglu influence vector is analyzed separately and treated as exploratory, described under the version note below. The remaining 17 audit targets are characterized at methodology rigor level without independent data re-analysis. Every audit-target citation is verified against its publisher record for title, authors, DOI, and the cited claim text. Contents of the deposit: analysis/: Python implementation of the audit's re-analysis pipeline: BACI parsing and corpus fitting, BEA 1997 Use Table reconstruction, SUSB binned-data MLE via Virkar-Clauset 2014, Vuong likelihood-ratio tests, Broido-Clauset 2019 corpus classification, semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit, the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity engine, and cross-validation of the Acemoglu first-order out-degree re-analysis against the published Alstott et al. 2014 powerlaw Python library, where fitted exponents and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances match to four decimal places. The influence-vector exponent reflects that library's default parameter-range cap at 3.0 and is treated as exploratory; the closed-form maximum-likelihood value on the same input lies above 3. outputs/: JSON output files containing per-target fitted parameters, x_min values, KS distances, bootstrap p-values, Vuong test statistics, and corpus aggregate statistics, plus the powerlaw-library cross-validation output and the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity results. audit_records/: per-target audit records for the three re-analyzed datasets (Acemoglu et al. 2012, Liu-Shen-Tan 2021, Axtell 2001), including methodology grade, data acquisition tier, sample sizes, fit details, and audit verdict. audit_targets/: structured audit-target list of all 20 verified entries with author, title, venue, year, DOI, verification status, data tier, methodology rigor level, and re-analysis results. verification_protocol.md: the citation-verification procedure used to assemble the audit population. references.md: the manuscript's numbered reference list. figures/: three figures from the manuscript, the BACI corpus alpha distributions, the Acemoglu d_i CCDF with fitted power law, and the SUSB firm-size CCDF with fitted power law. README.md: file inventory, dependency versions, reproducibility instructions, and citation guidance. CHANGELOG.md: version history of this deposit. LICENSE: MIT License (code), CC-BY 4.0 (documentation). Data sources used by the audit code are public and free: the BEA 1997 detailed Use Table (Bureau of Economic Analysis), the BACI HS92 Y2024 release (CEPII), and the SUSB 2017 US enterprise-size brackets (US Census Bureau). items.summary: Replication package for the paper 'Immaterial Apart, Material Together: Statement-Level Disclosure Regulation under Cheap Machine Aggregation'. items.summary: Code and experimental evidence supporting Calibrated Residual Tube Projection During Conditional Diffusion Sampling for Thermal Time Series , by Hyojin Park and Jinhong Yang (corresponding author). The release contains the selected B6 checkpoint, original method implementations, exact simulator and score settings, frozen selections, per-context evaluation records, diagnostic analyses, frozen detector coefficients, author-created figures, and a simulator reconstruction fixture. CPU audits verify saved aggregates, paired intervals, event metrics, decision criteria, cohort separation, journal chains, file hashes, and eight reconstructed fit trajectories. The study uses one fixed noiseless two-node thermal simulator and one selected diffusion generator. Repeated correction reduced true-equation residual by 11.07% and 10.53% on two three-stream cohorts, while both failed the original event-preservation and rollback criteria. A separate controlled detector showed lower T2 timing loss with corrected-only than raw-only synthetic training; real-only training retained lower loss. Deterministic ridge regression nearly recovered the simulator response. Original and later evaluation criteria remain distinguished. This is an evidence and code companion, not a self-contained one-command full retraining release. Full generated-trajectory arrays, other adapters' weights, the manuscript, internal authoring files, and AI-Hub source data are excluded. Historical runners retain original paths and execution gates. The measured-battery branch is represented by derived applicability counts only; no real-battery warning efficacy or broad physical generalization is claimed. License scope: original Python source in dt_diffpinn/ and tools/ is MIT; original synthetic data, results, model weights, figures, documentation, and metadata are CC BY 4.0. These licenses apply to their respective file categories. Third-party dependencies and AI-Hub data are not redistributed or relicensed. No journal acceptance or article publication is asserted. items.summary: This dataset contains the processed shot-event data, engineered features, and analysis outputs supporting the manuscript "Uncovering Global Football Scoring Structures Through Symbolic Regression and Similarity Networks" (Cengiz, M.A., Ebrahim, E.A., Alharthi, A., & Kara, M.), currently under review at Expert Systems with Applications . The study applies symbolic regression (PySR) and similarity-network analysis to shot-level event data from ten major football competitions to uncover interpretable mathematical structures underlying goal-scoring opportunities. Contents Copa_America_raw_shots — 790 raw shot events from 32 Copa América matches, retrieved via the statsbombpy API (competition_id = 223, season_id = 282). All original StatsBomb event fields are included; nested fields (location, freeze frame, tactics, etc.) have been flattened to plain text for spreadsheet compatibility. This subsample was used for the multicollinearity (VIF) diagnostic reported in the manuscript's Supplementary Material. Engineered_features — The 40-column engineered feature table (shot geometry, goal-frame geometry, tactical context, temporal, and interaction features) derived from the shot events above, as described in Section 3.3 of the manuscript. Original_final_results — Model comparison results (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, Expected Calibration Error, runtime) across all ten competitions and all benchmark/proposed models. Original_similarity_matrix — The pairwise symbolic similarity matrix across the ten competitions used to construct the similarity network and hierarchical taxonomy (Section 4.7–4.8). A README sheet with column-level descriptions and provenance notes is included in the workbook. Data source and attribution The underlying shot-event data were obtained from StatsBomb Open Data ( https://github.com/statsbomb/open-data ), made freely available by StatsBomb for research and non-commercial analytical use. In accordance with the StatsBomb Open Data usage terms, any research, analysis, or derivative work based on this data should cite StatsBomb as the original data source. This deposit provides the authors' own derived features, model outputs, and analysis results; it is intended as a companion resource to the associated manuscript and does not alter the terms under which the original StatsBomb data are made available.

items.summary: Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To evaluate ScientistTwo's capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result, ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/
items.title: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI

items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. items.summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
items.title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

items.summary: Online particle-filter OSSE diagnostics and experiment code for AMOC reconstruction. Data and analysis code underlying Fallah, Huiskamp and Goosse, pypfda v1.0: An open-source, model-agnostic particle-filter engine for online sequential paleo data assimilation in Earth system models (Geoscientific Model Development, in review). v2.0 supersedes v1.7 for every data-assimilation result. The cluster orchestrator used for v1.7 and earlier cloned member restart directories in slot order without first snapshotting the parents, so a parent's slot could be overwritten before all of its children had been copied and the ensemble that ran deviated from the systematic draw the filter logged. All nine DA experiments were re-run with a corrected driver that snapshots every parent before any clone. TRUTH, the free-running ensembles and the pseudo-observations never resample and are reused byte-identically, so every DA-versus-FREE comparison remains like-for-like; the re-extraction reproduces the unchanged free-running anchors exactly (diverse initial conditions r = −0.143, similar r = +0.520). Headline results. Over 100 years with diverse initial conditions and five-year assimilation cycles, assimilating 59 synthetic sea-surface-temperature proxies recovers the Atlantic overturning at r = +0.54 against a free-running ensemble at r = −0.14 (Δr = +0.68, 95 % CI [+0.40, +0.94]). An independent 300-year experiment with the same protocol gives r = +0.78 against +0.04 (Δr = +0.74, N eff ≈ 52, phase-randomisation p = 1×10 −5 , MSSS +0.58 versus −0.02). Note on the surface-air-temperature skill entries. The truth's atmosphere output for model year 1806 is missing. The loader used before 18 September 2026 dropped that year silently, which shifted the SAT truth by one year from 1807 on; the SAT skill maps and the sat_* entries of significance/v2_numbers.json in this version were recomputed with the truth aligned in time ( scripts/figscripts_v2/truth_align.py ). SST and AMOC results are unaffected. The figure scripts of the manuscript are deposited in scripts/figscripts_v2/ ; the maps draw the tripolar ocean grid at its true cell positions. Contents. AMOC and subpolar-gyre SST ensembles for the eight 100-year campaign arms and the 300-year run; per-cycle effective sample size, importance weights, resampling events, spread and full genealogy; the campaign significance family with its exhaustive circular-shift, Fourier phase-randomisation and block-permutation nulls; reliability and ancestor-divergence diagnostics; the 59-site pseudo-observation network; the idealised Lorenz sweeps; the SODA 2.2.4 derived series used for the observational consistency check; the nine run configurations; the corrected orchestrator and the campaign tooling that made the re-run auditable, including the unit test of the copy-step fix; and every analysis script. significance/v2_numbers.json is the single source from which every number in the manuscript is drawn. Reproducibility. bash regenerate_all.sh regenerates the campaign significance table byte-exactly, verified against MANIFEST.sha256 , and reprints the 300-year statistics, the online-versus-offline benchmark and the Lorenz parameter sweep from the deposited arrays alone. No model run and no cluster access are required. environment.yml pins the dependencies. What is not here. No CM2Mc-BLING source, executable, restart or input file is included; the model is not the authors' to redistribute, and run_configs/cm2mc/ carries only the namelists and one run log as proof of version. The raw coupled-model output (~16 TB) exceeds the capacity of any repository meeting the GMD archiving criteria and is available from the authors through the handling editor. Because the coupled model is not bit-for-bit reproducible across restarts, the diagnostics deposited here are the definitive record of the reported results. The engine itself is archived separately as 10.5281/zenodo.21281

items.summary: A mineral prospectivity map stacks geophysical, geochemical and structural evidence over a study area and outputs, per cell, the probability that a deposit is there. Such maps are typically presented with an area-under-curve (AUC) and a posterior, and both numbers can be inflated in two specific, well-understood ways. ProspectMap is an interactive tool that computes such a map by Weights of Evidence, a Bayesian log-odds update, and makes those two inflations first-class, measuring them rather than hiding them. This report quantifies both on the real US Midcontinent Mississippi-Valley-type zinc-lead belt (the open Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative dataset of Lawley et al., 2022) and on ten synthetic cases. The first inflation is evaluation: reporting AUC under random cross-validation, which lets spatially adjacent cells leak between train and test, overstates prospective skill. On the real belt, with thresholds, weights and prior fitted on the training folds only and every map cell scored, the Weights-of-Evidence AUC falls from 0.74 under random cross-validation to 0.65 under spatial block cross-validation, an inflation of 0.09, the second largest of the eleven cases. Under the same spatial folds a learned classifier reaches 0.91, but a baseline that ranks cells by their distance to the nearest training deposit reaches 0.90, so this protocol does not show that the classifier learned more than proximity to known deposits. The second inflation is modelling: Weights of Evidence assumes the evidence layers are conditionally independent given a deposit, and on the real belt they are not. The posterior probabilities sum to 1124 against 858 deposit cells (omnibus z = 8.3), so the posterior is overconfident. The six layers' contrasts are individually significant (studentized contrasts 2.45 to 5.80; exact one-sided p ≤ 1.9 × 10⁻³), but four of them come from thresholds that leave no deposit outside the pattern, where the weight outside the pattern is set by a zero-count correction. The tool displays the spatial-CV AUC, the conditional-independence test and the per-layer significance beside the inflated values; every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive tool and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_ProspectMap . Interactive tool: https://prospectmap.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative US Mississippi-Valley-type Zn-Pb belt dataset (Lawley et al. 2022, doi:10.1016/j.oregeorev.2021.104635).
items.title: ProspectMap: The Two Ways a Mineral Prospectivity Map Lies, Quantified on the Real US Mississippi-Valley-Type Belt

items.summary: This work studies how small perturbations of the Enchan local time-rate field propagate through fine spatial structure in the same field. The problem is motivated by the hard-wall boundary used in a previous Enchan two-route interference study: rather than imposing a primitive material opacity or an S=0 wall, the present work asks whether finite structure in the Enchan field itself can generate scale-selective transmission and reflection. Starting from the reduced finite-tension branch S_tt = div[mu(D) grad S] - S with mu(D) = 1/(1 + D^(3/2)), the field is decomposed as a structured background plus a small propagating perturbation. Stage A uses a predeclared one-dimensional frozen structured background and compares it with a matched smooth/homogenized control. The response is banded rather than a monotonic low-pass: long-scale perturbations remain comparatively transmissive while strong reflection bands appear when the perturbation resolves the fine structure. At ka = 2 the mean Stage-A structured transmission is approximately 6.25e-4 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.989; at ka = 4 the structured transmission is approximately 1.07e-14 while the smooth control remains approximately 0.962. Stage B replaces the hand-constructed surrogate with three previously frozen source-free Enchan final states from the published localized-field study. The source files are SHA-256 checked against the original run manifest before analysis. All three source profiles remain within the declared positive longitudinal branch and reproduce a scale-dependent structured-versus-smooth transmission difference. The largest Stage-B mean differences occur near ka = 1.0 and 1.5, where structured transmission is approximately 0.330 and 0.358 while the smooth controls remain approximately 0.994 and 0.988. The maximum Stage-B conservation residual is approximately 1.89e-15. Stage C extends the test to a full three-dimensional propagation study using the same three previously frozen source-free Enchan field configurations. A total of 54 cases were evaluated across structured, smooth, and vacuum controls, three selected spatial scales, and both normal and 30° oblique incidence. The scale-dependent scattering observed in the one-dimensional diagnostics persists in three dimensions. Structured backgrounds show reduced forward transmission together with increased reflection and lateral scattering relative to the matched controls. At ka = 4 under normal incidence, the mean structured transmission is approximately 0.486, compared with approximately 0.527 for the smooth control and 0.532 for vacuum. The maximum three-dimensional energy-accounting residual remains below 1.2% across all 54 cases. The result supports a model-level statement: fine S-field structure can act as a wavelength-selective barrier for small time-rate perturbations within the declared linearized Enchan branch. It does not identify ordinary matter with the tested surrogate or source-free structures, does not claim monotonic high-frequency blocking, and does not claim that a macroscopic material wall has been reconstructed. The Zenodo deposit contains the Version 1.1 manuscript PDF together with the complete reproducibility package for Stages A, B, and C, including the frozen numerical code, Stage-C configuration, archived source states, full numerical results, summary tables, execution manifest, README, LICENSE, and SHA-256 integrity records. The manuscript PDF is generated directly from the final Version 1.1 TeX source and is set as the default Zenodo preview. Version 1.1 update: Version 1.1 adds the completed Stage-C three-dimensional validation, updates the manuscript and reproducibility package accordingly, and preserves the Stage-A and Stage-B results unchanged. items.summary: A 3D city model is only as accurate as its building heights, and a model built from open data mostly infers those heights, from a mapped floor count, a height raster or a default value, rather than taking them from a mapped height. Maqueta reconstructs real places from open geospatial layers, with terrain from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model, building footprints and roads from Overture Maps, water, green areas and rail from OpenStreetMap, population from GHS-POP, and building heights from the Google Open Buildings 2.5D raster where it has coverage, and it records for every building how its height was obtained. Across the 118 baked places and 4.05 million buildings, 8.8% of heights come from a mapped height attribute, 6.4% from a mapped floor count, 73.2% from the Open Buildings 2.5D height raster, itself a model estimate from satellite imagery, and 11.6% from a default prior of 8 m. A public LoD2 reference exists for two of the places, both in the Netherlands, where the raster has no coverage. Against the 3D BAG, the fused heights have a root-mean-square error of 3.1 m at Delft, with a bias of -0.1 m, and of 8.3 m at Amsterdam, with a bias of -6.6 m; the Amsterdam figure rests on 50 reference buildings. The raster heights, which supply most of the buildings, are not validated by this benchmark, and public ground truth for open-data building heights is scarce. items.summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
items.title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
items.title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

items.summary: Recently, the bilingual advantage hypothesis has come under debate, and the replicability of studies documenting cognitive differences between bilingual and monolingual individuals has been questioned. These methodological concerns highlight the necessity for replication studies in bilingualism research. Furthermore, studies examining the relationship between bilingualism and event-based prospective memory (EB-PM) remain scarce. Building on this gap, the present study offers a partial replication of Yörük et al.’s (2023) research investigating the effect of bilingualism on EB-PM in a North Macedonian sample. Unlike the original study, in which bilingual participants were Turkish and English speakers residing in North Macedonia, both groups were selected from Türkiye. Additionally, task parameters were updated to resolve the high-saliency issue in the non-focal condition. A total of 98 young adults (49 per-group), aged 18-30 and residing in Ankara, were evaluated using focal and non-focal EB-PM tasks alongside an ongoing task. The 2 (Group: bilingual, monolingual) x 2 (Task type: focal, non-focal) mixed-design ANOVA results, consistent with the original study, provided no support for a bilingual advantage in PM accuracy. A significant main effect of task type emerged, with PM-accuracy in the focal task exceeding that of the non-focal task. Bilingual participants also responded significantly faster than monolinguals on the ongoing task, replicating the original findings. The findings suggest that any potential bilingual advantage in PM performance is context-dependent and dynamic. Furthermore, it was discussed that these findings indicate how language interaction context shapes the magnitude of observed effects within the framework of the Adaptive-Control-Hypothesis.
items.title: Re-examining the Bilingual Advantage in Prospective Memory: A Partial Replication with Turkish Bilingual and Monolingual Young Adults

items.summary: Revision of the dataset prepared during peer review of the accompanying data descriptor at IEEE Data Descriptions . The 94 satellite–in-situ pairs and their concentration values are unchanged; what changes is how records are identified in time, what per-reservoir metadata is provided, and what guidance ships with the raw processor columns. Breaking change samples.csv no longer has a Date column. It is replaced by Campaign , with the values Summer YYYY and Autumn YYYY . The monitoring network samples these reservoirs twice a year, in June and in November, and the campaign label is what the compiled matchup table retains; the literal dates in v1.0.0 were a downstream conversion and should not be read as acquisition timestamps. Code written against v1.0.0 must be updated. Per-record acquisition timestamps were not retained when the table was compiled, so the individual in-situ/satellite temporal offsets cannot be recovered from these files. What is documented is the characterisation reported with the original processing (Cuartero et al., 2023): all 94 images fall inside the ±48 h selection window and 26% were acquired on the same day as the in-situ sample. Records cannot be filtered by temporal offset; studies for which simultaneity is critical should treat the whole collection as subject to an offset of up to two days. Added metadata.csv gains two morphometric descriptors per reservoir (15 → 17 columns): Eq. width (pix) , the equivalent width √A in 10 m pixels, and Window fraction (%) , the share of the water surface covered by a single 7×7 extraction window. Across the network the window fraction ranges from 0.26% to 49%. Users are advised to discard or treat separately any reservoir above about 25%. baseline_correction.py , a self-contained script (NumPy and pandas only) that fits a log–log correction log10(Chl) = a·log10(P) + b for each processor, plus a joint form over the three co-registered retrievals, and evaluates it under leave-one-reservoir-out cross-validation. Out-of-sample, it brings C2X from 639% to 39% MAPD and C2XC from 2181% to 43%; the joint form reaches 18%. It is a starting point and a sanity check, not a recommended retrieval, and its coefficients should not be transferred to other networks without refitting. Changed README updated for the new columns and the script, with a provenance note on time and a note on modelling with unevenly sampled reservoirs (Gini 0.32; effective number of equally weighted reservoirs 21.9 of 32). Use the reservoir, not the record, as the unit of resampling. The dataset is now named C2NEx-22, and the accompanying descriptor is identified as submitted to IEEE Data Descriptions .
items.title: C2NEx-22: A Paired Satellite–in-situ Chlorophyll-a in Extremadura, Spain for 32 Reservoirs Dataset

items.summary: This dataset supports the study “Disassembly access to CRM recovery targets in consumer robot vacuums”. It contains target-level coding records for 85 qualifying physical targets across nine used consumer robot vacuums, the derived class-by-unit access matrix, analytical coding rules, and provenance records supporting the reported disassembly-access analysis. Five predefined CRM-relevant component classes were assessed: energy storage, locomotion, cleaning actuation, control electronics, and sensing and navigation. The analytical endpoint was independent separation of each qualifying target as an identifiable assembly. Target-level records report removal outcomes and the interface condition at the target boundary required for independent separation. The dataset does not verify the CRM composition or quantity of individual assemblies. Target multiplicity differed by class and product architecture; pooled target counts are descriptive and should not be interpreted as market-level prevalence or removal-rate estimates. Original teardown photographs and video records are not included in the public dataset; source identifiers are retained for provenance, and original media may be available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
items.title: Dataset for LCE 2027

items.summary: Our earlier note (rejected from an SC26 AI4S workshop, subsequently published as AIIT Bulletin Vol. 20) compared classical reduced-order models (POD, DMD) against naive neural surrogates (a fully-connected network, a CNN) on textbook-scale problems (lid-driven cavity, dam-break), on a single consumer GPU workstation. That note left five concrete gaps: no graph-based neural baseline, no industrially complex geometry, weak statistical evidence (nine snapshots, a single seed), no learned-dynamics counterpart to DMD, and no hyperparameter search for the neural baselines. This paper closes four of those five. The test case is an industrially representative two-phase stirred tank — a six-blade rotating impeller on a sliding (AMI) mesh, a bottom sparger injecting gas into water, ∼167k cells, solved with OpenFOAM's twoPhaseEulerFoam — run entirely on a single Mac Studio (Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, no discrete GPU). We benchmark five methods (POD, DMD, a neural network, a Graph Neural Operator, and a Deep Koopman autoencoder) on a genuine extrapolation task, backed by a 400-run statistical-robustness sweep, hyperparameter searches for both neural baselines, a check across three impeller speeds, and a four-level forcing-irregularity sweep (quasi-periodic through chaotic, direction-reversing impeller motion) intended to locate DMD's failure point. DMD wins consistently across every data scale, truncation choice, operating condition, and forcing-irregularity level tested, at both a 1 s and an extended 3 s prediction horizon – we did not find the failure threshold we went looking for, and report that directly. The search was not wasted, however: a Deep Koopman autoencoder, competitive at 1 s, degrades sharply at 3 s from compounding autoregressive rollout error (exposure bias); two independent, cheap mitigations – a physical [0, 1] clip mirroring the Graph Neural Operator's own implicit stabilization, and multi-step scheduled-sampling training – each recover roughly a third to a half of the gap without closing it, confirming the diagnosis. A separate, unplanned check turns up a sharper result: ranking methods by mass conservation rather than per-cell accuracy reorders them completely, with the most accurate method (DMD) only third-best at holding a basic physical invariant. We treat all three investigations as concrete instances of a broader, practical question for this community: how much genuine, open-ended scientific investigation — not just a fixed benchmark — can a single high-end workstation support before an HPC allocation is actually necessary? All code, case files, and Colab notebooks are released on GitHub for reproduction.
items.title: How Far Does One Workstation Go? A Pre-HPC Efficiency Check for Industrial-Scale CFD and Reduced-Order Model Benchmarking

items.summary: FlowMLLab v1.7.0 adds paired self-supervised wake-learning modules. Week 7.3 retains the strong gappy-POD baseline on masked low-rank wake reconstruction and corrects linear-probe pooling and sample-standard-deviation reporting. Week 7.4 generates sixteen compact Reynolds trajectories and measures target-label efficiency for instantaneous lift using frozen pretrained, random and POD-32 representations. Full trajectory splits, source-label selection costs, per-case errors, data hashes and coarse-CFD limitations are disclosed. The course includes 42 notebooks and 26 PDF lectures through Week 15. This is a MAPA-inspired educational experiment, not a reproduction of its neuroscience benchmark.
items.title: FlowMLLab: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible CFD-to-Scientific-Machine-Learning Experiments

items.summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.
items.title: From Historical Tabular Image to Knowledge Graphs: A Provenance-Aware Modular Pipeline

items.summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: Geospatial foundation models can provide strong flood-segmentation performance, but their size limits deployment on memory-constrained edge hardware. We distill a 300-million-parameter Prithvi-EO-2.0 teacher, fine-tuned on the 252 manually labeled Sen1Floods11 training scenes, into a 0.7-million-parameter EfficientViT-B0 student. The teacher supervises additional unlabeled Sentinel-2 imagery, allowing the student training set to grow without new manual annotations. At the matched budget of 252 scenes, teacher-supervised training is competitive with direct training and improves STURM-Flood performance across tested configurations; a geometry-matched control shows that label source alone does not explain the difference. Scaling the teacher-supervised pool to 2,500 scenes narrows the remaining student--teacher gap: the float student reaches 0.787 water intersection over union on the Sen1Floods11 test split against 0.822 for the teacher, matches the teacher on STURM-Flood under our evaluation protocol, and remains below it on WorldFloods-v2. After activation replacement and quantization-aware training, the student runs as a 1.5-megabyte 8-bit integer (INT8) TensorRT engine on a Jetson Xavier NX at 5.57 milliseconds of graphics processing unit (GPU) compute per 512-by-512 image, with approximately 14 megabytes of runtime device memory. A fixed modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI) threshold is competitive with both models on the two clean external benchmarks, so we interpret those benchmarks as generalization tests rather than as evidence of learned-model superiority over a spectral rule. The results support the conclusion: foundation-model supervision can amplify a fixed manual annotation budget into a substantially larger training set and yield a compact, deployable edge model.
items.title: Cross-Architecture Foundation-Model Distillation for Edge Flood Segmentation

items.summary: Supplementary repository accompanying the preprint 'General-Purpose Audio Foundation Models Improve Zero-Adaptation Cross-Water Transfer in Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition' (to appear as Preprints 2026; preprint v1.3, September 2026). This archive fulfills the preprint's Data Availability statement: upon preprint release it deposits the full evaluation and analysis code; 126 per-cell metric JSONs (within-corpus probes, 72-pair cross-corpus zero-shot transfer, VTUAD v1.2.0-label re-probes); aggregate bootstrap and protocol-audit JSONs; the o2q permutation-control numerics (5,000 runs per granularity: full F1 distributions, permuted label matrices, labels and recording ids); per-segment predictions for all 12 cross-transfer directions (FM probes and 3-seed + oracle ResNet-18 anchors); the Appendix B 12 x 6 matrix; the four-corpus audio index (258,893 segments, basenames only); figure sources; and the embedding caches of the series' own VTUAD corpus for all six models (uploaded as six per-model zips alongside the main archive). No raw audio is redistributed. Cached embeddings of the third-party corpora (ShipsEar, Oceanship, QiandaoEar22) are deliberately excluded under the data providers' terms (no redistribution of the data or derivative copies) and are exactly regenerable with the deposited scripts; every reported statistic can be verified from the deposited numeric artifacts. VTUAD itself: Zenodo concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22274549. A sha256 manifest (SHA256SUMS.txt) covers every file in the main archive. Version 2 supplement (2026-09-18): adds (a) the companion UDA benchmark's v2 seed-expansion target-oracle summary (aggregate statistics and per-seed results for all 12 directions: 10 seeds for the Oceanship-QiandaoEar22 two-domain matrix, 8 seeds for the seven VTUAD/ShipsEar-extension directions covered by the expansion, 3 original seeds for the three uncovered directions), which backs the target-oracle column of Table 4.3 of the preprint; (b) an environment file (requirements.txt); (c) a split-manifest and data-version note (per-corpus train/val/test segment counts, VTUAD v1.2.0 label-correction and QiandaoEar22 filename-collision documentation). All previously deposited artifacts are unchanged; the reported statistics are identical.
items.title: Supplementary repository: code, evaluation artifacts, and VTUAD embedding caches for 'General-Purpose Audio Foundation Models Improve Zero-Adaptation Cross-Water Transfer in Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition' (to appear as Preprints 2026)

items.summary: Depression and anxiety among university students have risen alongside problematic social media use, and while traditional interventions are effective, they face barriers to scalability and accessibility. AI-driven chatbots offer a scalable, real-time, anonymous alternative, with recent meta-analyses showing comparable reductions in depressive symptoms relative to standard interventions. This poster presents the protocol for a two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled non-inferiority trial evaluating whether a Social Media Wellness Chatbot is non-inferior to an active psychoeducational control in reducing depressive symptoms among high-risk university students (PHQ-9 ≥ 10, social media use ≥ 2 hrs/day). Approximately 320 students will be randomized 1:1 to the chatbot (CBT-based exercises, mood tracking, and social media habit coaching, 4-5x/week for 10-15 min/day) or a 6-week online psychoeducational toolkit ("Social Media and Mental Wellness Toolkit"). The primary outcome is change in PHQ-9 score from baseline to 6-week post-test, evaluated against a non-inferiority margin of Δ ≈ 3 points. Secondary outcomes include anxiety (GAD-7), stress (PSS), well-being (WHO-5), and engagement metrics. As this is a study protocol, results are not yet available. If non-inferiority is established, the chatbot's accessibility, scalability, and on-demand availability would support its integration into university mental health services. Presented at the First Annual HCAP (Health, Community, and Policy) Research Forum, University of Texas at San Antonio, April 25, 2025.
items.title: Social Media Wellness Chatbot for Students: A Randomized Controlled Non-Inferiority Trial Protocol of an AI-Driven Mental Health Intervention in High-Risk University Populations
